title: Doing the Right Thing for the Wrong Reason — Matthew 6:1
paragraphs: Doing the Right Thing for the Wrong Reason — Matthew 6:1

They applauded the act.
He rejected the motive.
That is the terror of Matthew 6:1.
You can do the right thing… and still be wrong before God.

Jesus said, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). The warning is not against righteousness. It is against performance. Not against obedience. Against exhibition. Not against good works. Against hungry hearts fishing for human worship.

That means a man can give generously and still be starving for applause.
A woman can serve faithfully and still be secretly building her own throne.
A preacher can say holy words while craving unholy attention.

Because sometimes the sin is not in what we did.
The sin is in why we did it.

Jesus is not merely exposing fake religion. He is rescuing us from it. He is pulling us out of the exhausting prison of needing to be seen, praised, validated, and admired. He is telling us that the Father sees what the crowd cannot. And what the Father rewards is not polished image—but surrendered truth.
This is where grace walks in.

Because if God only accepted pure motives, who among us could stand? Our hearts are mixed. Our intentions wobble. Even our best moments can smell like pride. But Jesus lived the life we could not live—perfect in action, perfect in motive, perfect in secret devotion to the Father. Then He went to the cross for hypocrites, attention-seekers, image-builders, and sinners like us. He did not die for your polished reputation. He died for your real heart.

Not just of bad deeds.
Repent of borrowed holiness.
Repent of public righteousness with private vanity.
Repent of turning ministry into self-promotion.
Because in Jesus, you do not have to perform to be loved. You do not have to be noticed to be valuable. You do not have to be praised to be secure. The Father already sees you through the Son.

Do the right thing.
But do it for the right King.
And when no one claps, no one posts, no one notices, and no one rewards you on earth—heaven still sees. The Father still knows. Christ is still enough.
